Jang’s score, mixing electronic and orchestral elements, moving freely from mournful to menacing, and contributing immeasurably to the film’s mounting momentum, is among his very finest.

screenings.title: Heathers
screenings.description: “Dear Diary: My teen-angst bullshit now has a body count.” A caustic rejoinder to John Hughes’s ’80s Brat Pack pictures, Lehmann’s savage suburban satire brought out the sociopathic side of Christian Slater’s too-cool outlaw persona, casting him as J.D., the motorcycle-riding new arrival at Ohio’s Westerburg High School who recruits Winona Ryder’s at-first pliable Veronica Chandler into his increasingly unhinged plans to humble their class’s ruling clique of three terrible popular girls named Heather. Clearly having a ball with Daniel Waters’s imminently quotable, coal-black screenplay, Ryder gives more than a few line-readings for the ages here; just try to keep “What’s your damage?” out of your vocabulary after viewing.

screenings.title: The Double
screenings.description: Inspired by the Dostoyevsky novella of the same title, Ayoade’s noir-inflected sophomore feature gives a dead game Jesse Eisenberg not one but two juicy parts as both a mousy, long-overlooked office drone, Simon James, and his new colleague, the cocksure and charismatic James Simon, who no one other than Simon seems to notice is in fact Simon’s doppelgänger, and who briskly sets about invading every aspect of Simon’s life. The bleakly comic story of a man struggling to get the upper hand over himself, with Eisenberg, in his virtuoso double role, getting more than capable backup from a supporting cast that includes Mia Wasikowska, Wallace Shawn, and Cathy Moriarty.

screenings.title: Small Change
screenings.description: From first kisses to more sinister secrets, all of the loneliness and wonderment and danger and astonishing endurance that distinguish the years we pass between infancy and adolescence are contained here in Truffaut’s string of loosely connected vignettes concerning a group of schoolchildren living in the provincial town of Thiers in central France and their very involved instructor (Jean-François Stévenin). A film brimming with pleasures for children and adults both, unmistakably sweet-spirited while refreshingly free of sentimental treacle. “A comedy, a romance, a mystery—in a word: childhood—captured, distilled, and transformed effortlessly from sketchbook to symphony in the hands of a master.” —Wes Anderson

screenings.title: High and Low
screenings.description: Kurosawa’s formal genius and rare humanism are on full display in this white-knuckle thriller—source of an upcoming remake by Spike Lee—which transposes the materials of an Ed McBain novel to contemporary Japan, starring Toshiro Mifune as a rich industrialist thrown into a nerve-shredding situation after, first believing his son has been kidnapped, discovering that his chauffeur’s child was taken by accident. Boasting nigh-constant visual invention, geometric precision of framing, an inventive narrative structure, and a bevy of staggering set pieces—the train hand-off! the down-and-dirty G.I. bar!—High & Low is a virtuoso work that’s also a deeply moral one, exploring the meaning of “justice” in a society defined by vast economic disparity.

screenings.title: Bird in Hand + Q&A
screenings.description: Inspired by Roscher’s own biracial experience, BIRD IN HAND follows the newly engaged Bird Rowe (Alisha Wainwright) as she returns to her rural hometown to plan the wedding with her narcissistic hippie mother Carlotta (Christine Lahti). Bird also has a hidden agenda, one that leads her to her mother’s new neighbors, a misguided couple on a mission to ‘rebrand’ a plantation. Truth, lies, and fantasy collide against that backdrop, leading to a surprising climax as tender as it is funny.

screenings.title: The Practice of Love
screenings.description: Export’s third feature is a feminist upending of film noir conceits starring Adelheid Arndt as a journalist who uncovers a murderous conspiracy that, upon further investigation, may very well have a connection to her unhappy personal life. “An anti-romance in which the heroine, oscillating between two relationships, gradually discovers that both are impossible, not because the subjective processes of ‘love’ are defective, but because the objective, social matrix in which both her male lovers operate is corrupt, immoral, murderous: in this film, the male world and its power structures cancel the possibility of love beyond the matter of sexuality, that is the objectification of love. Export makes use of techniques drawn from her earlier experimental cinema, video and conceptual photography to expand the possibilities of narrative feature filmmaking and to disintegrate some of its overdetermined conventions.” —Gary Indiana

screenings.title: Nostos: The Return
screenings.description: Rather than weighing the merits of one translation of The Odyssey against those of another, Piavoli dispenses with language—or, at least, readily comprehensible language—altogether, giving us an interpretation of the Homeric epic that is first and foremost a sensual, audiovisual experience, what dialogue there is spoken in a hotchpotch of ancient Thessalonian Greek, Sanskrit, and Latin. Free of the anxiety of influence, Piavoli—in his first foray into fiction filmmaking in a career that stretches back to the 1950s—transforms his source into a lyric memory piece, difficult to describe, impossible to forget, and at times positively overwhelming in its beauty.

screenings.title: Valie Export Shorts Program
screenings.description: A provocative program of short films by Export whose work, focused in her words, on “the body and moreover the female body,” can be viewed as both parallel to and a response against that of the male-dominated Viennese Actionists. Featuring the confrontational and mock-erotic Self-Portrait with Head; Touch Cinema, a document of Export’s taboo-busting performance piece; Man & Woman & Animal, an “assertion and affirmation of female sexuality and its independence from male values and pleasures” [Joanna Kierman]; Syntagma, a frenzied study of the fragmented female form; and Lust, per the director “a continuation of my previous work with the body as a vehicle for social codes.

screenings.title: Common Carrier | Four by James N. Kienitz Wilkins
screenings.description: A collection of vignettes and conversations with various full-time and part-time artists, several featuring Wilkins himself, the kaleidoscopic Common Carrier’s images are almost entirely “overlapped,” as are its dialogues, which among other things address schizophrenia, mystical “aura,” division of labor, and constitutional law, these varied discussions sharing the soundtrack with disparate radio feeds from WNYC and Hot 97 that are united by the recurrence of the word “work.” A rich and ruminative film about making do in the 21st century, eking out a creative existence in the scant free time that’s left over after the other obligations have been met.

screenings.title: Concessions + Q&A
screenings.description: Q&A with Writer/Director Mas Bouzidi and actors Josh Hamilton, Rob Riordan, Jonathan Lorenzo Price, and Lana Rockwell following the 10/4 screening of Bouzidi's debut feature, Concessions (2025). The discussion will be moderated by Charlotte Wells (director of Aftersun).

screenings.title: O Brother, Where Art Thou?
screenings.description: The Coens’ country-fried, Depression era, quasi-musical take on The Odyssey borrows its title—and more than a bit of its anarchic sense of humor—from Preston Sturges’s Sullivan’s Travels, choreography cues from Busby Berkeley, and rips a few dozen pages out of the Great American Songbook for good measure. Pomaded convict Everett Ulysses McGill (George Clooney) takes a powder from a Mississippi chain gang with dimwit pals John Turturro and Tim Blake Nelson in tow and sets out to scare up his Penelope (Holly Hunter), along the way running afoul of Klansmen, gangsters, sultry creek-side sirens, and a Bible-thumping Cyclops (John Goodman), even taking a quick break en route to record a jubilant rendition of “Man of Constant Sorrow.”

screenings.title: RoboCop - The Director's Cut
screenings.description: I’d buy that for a dollar! For a strange few years, beginning with this runaway hit, the perverse imagination and earthy humor of Verhoeven seemed to sync up perfectly with the desires of the American multiplex-going public. In dystopian Detroit, private sector Omni Consumer Products have taken over policing and made the ultimate law enforcement machine from leftover pieces of peace officer Peter Weller—but they didn’t bank on their invention making his way up the corporate ladder of crime. A frightfully funny vision of a post-industrial cybernetic future, with Kurtwood Smith, Ronny Cox, and Muguel Ferrer an impressive trifecta of irredeemable scumbags.

screenings.title: Wings of Desire
screenings.description: In Wim Wenders’ iconic Wings of Desire, two angels, Damiel and Cassiel, glide through the streets of a divided Berlin, observing the bustling population. When Damiel falls in love with lonely trapeze artist Marion, the angel longs to experience life in the physical world. Featuring a showstopping performance by a young Nick Cave, crooning the title track from From Her to Eternity, Wings of Desire is one of the most inexhaustible modern films.

Chronovisor
screenings.description: While writing a monograph on historical theories of memory, Béatrice (Anne Laure Sellier), a respected academic, becomes beguiled by the allegedly true story of the Chronovisor, an occult device said to reproduce visuals from any point in history on a TV screen. Her obsession with the mysterious machine drags her from her Upper East Side apartment through the depths of New York City’s hidden libraries, to the edge of a breakthrough.

screenings.description: Tehran, 1958. After his beloved violin is broken, renowned musician Nasser Ali Khan loses his desire to live. Confined to bed, he drifts through memories and dreams of his youth, his family, and the great lost love that inspired his music…

screenings.title: On a String + Q&A
screenings.description: Isabel (Isabel Hagen) is a young, Juilliard-trained violist still living at home with her parents in the heart of New York City. She’s trying to make a living playing gigs with her friends but when her toxic ex- boyfriend reappears, who also happens to be the Philharmonic’s “newest, hottest cellist,” he informs her of a viola opening in the prestigious orchestra. Nothing can go wrong, right?

screenings.title: All the Mornings of the World + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: An ambitious young musician’s life becomes entwined with that of his reclusive master in director Alain Corneau’s haunting portrait of composer Marin Marais and his teacher, Monsieur de Sainte-Colombe. With a landmark score by Jordi Savall–whose viola da gamba recordings inspired novelist Pascal Quignard’s original story–Tous les Matins du Monde is a transporting meditation on artistic devotion, memory, and longing.

screenings.title: The Downtown Festival: ART/New York & 3 Downtown Artists  + Q&A
screenings.description: ABOUT THE DOWNTOWN FESTIVAL: The Downtown Festival is a multidisciplinary celebration of independent film, music, art, and culture held across Lower Manhattan each October. Founded and directed by filmmaker Rebekah Sherman-Myntti, the festival brings together artists across disciplines and generations through film premieres, anniversary screenings, live music performances, artist talks, and special one-night-only events. Programming is led by Sherman-Myntti and Associate Director Briana Bursten, with a focus on discovery, experimentation, community, and genuine artist-to-artist exchange. The festival’s film program runs October 9-18 at Roxy Cinema, with additional programming and special events taking place all over downtown.

screenings.title: Prison + Who Are You Dorothy Dean? Book Launch and Q&A
screenings.description: Éditions 1989 celebrates the launch of the second edition of Who Are You Dorothy Dean?, the first book devoted to the late African American writer and actress. When Dorothy Dean (1932–1987) entered the 1960s New York underground scene, she quickly became one of its key figures—starring in six of Andy Warhol’s films and inspiring the likes of Robert Mapplethorpe and Robert Creeley.

screenings.title: The Red Violin + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: Following the success of 1993’s Thirty Two Short Films About Glenn Gould, director François Girard and co-writer Don McKellar reunited to tell the story of The Red Violin, tracing the titular instrument’s journey from its creation in 17th-century Italy to an auction in 1990s Montreal–and the various musicians and owners it bewitches along the way. Girard mounts a handsome production with location shooting across five countries, from China to Austria, and Samuel L. Jackson shines as Charles Morritz, a fussy instrument appraiser who falls under the violin’s spell while decoding its secrets. Composer John Corigliano won the Academy Award for Best Original Score, and violinist Joshua Bell performed all of the solos in the film.

screenings.title: Nosferatu + Live Score
screenings.description: Nosferatu + Live Score by the Andrew Alden Ensemble The vampire film that started them all gets its shadow back. The Andrew Alden Ensemble performs an original score live beneath F.W. Murnau’s 1922 landmark — the New York chamber group whose violin, cello, keys, drums, and voice sit somewhere between contemporary classical and rock, writing music built for the room rather than the recording booth: immediate, physical, and made for this film alone. On screen, Count Orlok (Max Schreck) uncoils out of the Carpathians — all talons and teeth and rat-borne plague — and crosses the sea toward a town that cannot wake from him. A hundred years later the images still crawl.

screenings.title: Vampyr + Live Score
screenings.description: Carl Theodor Dreyer’s 1932 fever dream is less a horror film than a nightmare filmed at the moment of waking — fog, drifting shadows, a scythe, a burial seen from inside the coffin. The Andrew Alden Ensemble scores it live with violin, electric guitar, piano, synthesizers, and percussion, the New York group’s music moving with the film’s logic of dread rather than against it. A young traveler, Allan Gray (Julian West), arrives in a riverside village held under the spell of a vampire, and the world begins to come loose at the edges. Dreyer made it as sound cinema was being born and produced something stranger than either silence or speech; performed with a live original score, it turns stranger still.

screenings.title: The Draughtsman's Contract + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: Set in a richly exaggerated 17th-century England, Peter Greenaway’s sumptuous and sensuously charged brainteaser catapulted him to the forefront of international art cinema. Adorned with intricate wordplay, extravagant costumes and opulent photography, Greenaway’s first narrative feature weaves a labyrinthine mystery around the maxim “draw what you see, not what you know.” An aristocratic wife (Janet Suzman) commissions a young, cocksure draughtsman (Anthony Higgins) to sketch her husband’s property while he is away—in exchange for a fee, room and board, and one sexual favor for each of the twelve drawings. As the draughtsman becomes more entrenched in the devious schemings in this seemingly idyllic country home, curious details emerge in his drawings that may reveal a murder.
screenings.country: Instruments of Desire Comedy, Drama, Mystery

screenings.title: Tár + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: From writer-producer-director Todd Field comes TÁR, starring Cate Blanchett as Lydia Tár, the celebrated chief conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic. We meet Tár at the height of her career, as she’s preparing both a book launch and a much-anticipated live recording of Mahler’s Fifth Symphony. Over the ensuing weeks, her life and career unravel as allegations of misconduct erode her carefully cultivated public image. The result is a searing examination of artistic authority, institutional politics, and the blurred boundary between mentorship and exploitation.
